steps.title: Every position in a text is a training example
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.1 · STEP 1 OF 14
Every position in a text is a training example

Training turns plain text into quiz questions: at every position, guess the next token. “The river bank flooded” gives three questions for free. Press Play.

WHAT IT IS

Pre-training is the first and biggest training phase: show the model huge amounts of text and, at every position, ask it to predict the next token. The text supplies the right answer, so no one has to label anything.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A cloze test that writes itself: cover every word of a book in turn and guess it from the words before. One book gives thousands of questions.
Technical
Turning a log into training rows with a sliding window: every prefix is a feature row, the next event is its label. One log stream yields one row per event.
Play ▶
The
river
bank
flooded
what the model sees
answer to guess
example 1	The →	river
example 2	The river →	bank
example 3	The river bank →	flooded
length of a text (tokens): 4

A text of 4 tokens gives 3 next-token examples. Llama 3 405B was trained on 15.6 trillion tokens: about 15.6 trillion examples, no human labels needed.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

A text of n tokens gives n − 1 examples. The model makes all of them in one forward pass: the vector at position i predicts token i + 1. Each example's probabilities come from the same logits → softmax you saw in Lesson 2.

EVIDENCE

GPT-1 states the objective directly: “we use a standard language modeling objective to maximize the following likelihood”: L1(U) = Σi log P(ui | ui−k, …, ui−1; Θ), one term per position. Radford et al., Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (2018) ↗ Llama 3's flagship was “pre-trained … on 15.6T text tokens”. The Llama 3 Herd of Models (2024) ↗

Go deeper

Real training cuts text into fixed-length windows (e.g. 4,096 or 8,192 tokens) and scores every position in the window at once. The text itself is the label, which is why this is called self-supervised learning.

steps.title: Loss: how surprised the model was by the right answer
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.1 · STEP 2 OF 14
Loss: how surprised the model was by the right answer

The loss is −log of the probability the model gave the correct token. Confident and right: near 0. Unsure: large. Train a step and watch the gradient push “flooded” up and the loss fall.

WHAT IT IS

The loss (here cross-entropy) is one number for how wrong the model was: loss = −ln p(correct token). Training means changing the weights to make the loss smaller, using the gradient (Lesson 1: which way each number should move to reduce the loss).

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A weather forecaster scored on what they said about the weather that happened. Said 90% rain and it rained: small penalty. Said 1%: huge penalty. Hedging on everything costs a medium penalty every day.
Technical
Log loss in a click-prediction model: the same formula, applied to the observed click. A confident wrong prediction is punished far more than a cautious one.

Here the step nudges the five scores directly. Real training nudges the billions of weights that produce the scores, using the same gradient sent backward through every layer (backpropagation).

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

With softmax, the gradient of the loss on each score is simply p − 1 for the correct token and p for every other: push the right answer up, push the rest down in proportion to how much they stole. Backpropagation carries that signal through all the layers to every weight.

EVIDENCE

Maximizing Σ log P(next token | earlier tokens) (GPT-1's stated objective) is exactly minimizing the summed −log loss on this page. Radford et al. (2018) ↗ And the loss falls predictably with scale: “The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training”. Kaplan et al., Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (2020) ↗

Go deeper

Why a log: probabilities of a whole text multiply, logs add, so the loss of a text is the sum over its positions. Lesson 2's trained model gives flooded 78% here: loss 0.25. Averaged over trillions of tokens, this one number is what pre-training drives down.

steps.title: The causal mask: no peeking at the answer
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.1 · STEP 3 OF 14
The causal mask: no peeking at the answer

Training feeds the whole sentence at once, so “bank” could simply look at “flooded” and copy it. The causal mask blocks every later position, so each token only looks backward. Toggle the mask.

WHAT IT IS

The causal mask is a triangle of “not allowed” entries in the attention grid: position i may attend to positions 1…i, never i + 1 onward. “Causal” because the past can influence the future, not the reverse.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Grading a crossword where each clue's answer is printed right next to it: you must cover the answers, or the test measures nothing.
Technical
Preventing look-ahead leakage in a time-series model: when you build features for time t, you only join rows with timestamps ≤ t, or the model scores perfectly offline and fails in production.

Mask on

Cheating: each row's answer sits just right of the diagonal (orange). “The” must guess “river” and puts 51% on “river”; “bank” must guess “flooded” and puts 57% on “flooded”. With training, these weights head to 100% and the loss to near zero: the model learns to copy, which is useless when generating: the next word doesn't exist yet.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

In code it's one addition before softmax: scores + mask, where the mask is 0 on and below the diagonal and −∞ above it. e−∞ = 0, so future tokens get exactly zero weight. Training runs all positions in parallel (fast); generation runs one at a time (Lesson 2), and the mask makes the two compute the same thing.

EVIDENCE

The transformer paper: “We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to −∞) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections” (section 3.2.3). Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017) ↗

Go deeper

This is why the KV cache works (Lesson 2): because a token never looks forward, its keys and values never change when later tokens arrive. The same mask that makes training honest makes caching safe.

steps.title: Scale: about 6 operations per parameter per token
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.1 · STEP 4 OF 14
Scale: about 6 operations per parameter per token

Training compute ≈ 6 × parameters × training tokens: 2 for the forward pass, about 4 for the backward pass. Pick a model and token count and see how many GPUs and days it takes.

WHAT IT IS

FLOPs (floating-point operations) count the multiply-adds. A forward pass costs about 2 per parameter per token (Lesson 2's prefill number); the backward pass (computing gradients) about twice that, so training ≈ 6. MFU (model FLOPs utilization) is the share of the GPUs' peak math actually used.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Building a dam versus running the hydroelectric plant: a one-off megaproject with a huge crew, then years of steady operation where every hour of running cost counts.
Technical
A massive one-off batch backfill on a whole cluster versus the online service that serves the result: one is judged by job completion time and utilization, the other by p99 latency and cost per request.
8B
70B
405B

H100 GPUs: 16,384

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Training splits the model and the data across thousands of GPUs that must exchange gradients every step, so the network and stragglers (the slowest GPU, which every step waits for) matter as much as the chips. Memory per parameter is several times the 16-bit weights (gradients, plus optimizer state: the extra numbers per weight the optimizer keeps, such as running averages of past gradients). One failed GPU stalls the whole synchronized job, so teams checkpoint often.

EVIDENCE

Kaplan et al.: “Accounting for the backwards pass (approximately twice the compute as the forwards pass), we then define the estimated non-embedding compute as C ≈ 6N floating point operators per training token.” Scaling Laws (2020) ↗ Llama 3 405B: “pre-trained using 3.8×1025 FLOPs”, “on up to 16K H100 GPUs”, at 38–43% BF16 MFU; “During a 54-day snapshot period of pre-training, we experienced a total of 466 job interruptions.” The Llama 3 Herd of Models (2024) ↗

Go deeper

Llama 3 405B: 6 × 405 billion × 15.6 trillion ≈ 3.8 × 10²⁵ operations, the figure Meta reports. On 16,384 H100s at 40% utilization that's about 68 days of pure compute; failures and restarts add more. Training is a giant batch job; serving is an online service.

steps.title: A base model only continues text
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.2 · STEP 5 OF 14
A base model only continues text

Pre-training makes a base model: it continues text the way the internet would, which isn't the same as answering. Post-training turns it into an assistant. Ask both the same question.

WHAT IT IS

A base model is the output of pre-training (1.7). Post-training is everything after: supervised fine-tuning and preference tuning (next two steps). A chat template wraps each turn in special tokens (like <|user|>, <|assistant|>) so the model can see who is speaking and where a turn ends.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A brilliant new hire who has read every document in the company but has never been told their job: ask a question and they recite related pages. Onboarding teaches them to answer.
Technical
A general-purpose text-completion engine versus the same engine behind a request/response protocol: the template is the wire format (headers and delimiters) that frames each message.
Base model (after 3.1)
Chat model (after 3.2)
What you typed
What the model actually reads
What is a river bank? What is a flood plain? What is a delta? Label each one on the map below, then answer questions 4 to 6.

Orange = generated (illustrative outputs). Teal = special tokens from the chat template: a base model wasn't trained to use them as turn markers; the chat model was trained on thousands of examples shaped exactly like this.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

The API's messages list is flattened into one token string with the template; the server appends the assistant header, and the model continues from there until it emits the end-of-turn token. SFT data is tiny next to pre-training's (Llama 2: 27,540 written SFT examples versus 2 trillion pre-training tokens), yet post-training decides how the model behaves.

EVIDENCE

Hugging Face's docs: “All causal LMs, whether chat-trained or not, continue a sequence of tokens. … training usually begins with ‘pre-training’ on a huge corpus of text, which creates a ‘base’ model.” Chat models see “control tokens like <|user|> or <|assistant|>”, and with the wrong ones “these models would have drastically worse performance.” Transformers: Chat templates ↗

Go deeper

On the internet, a question is often followed by more questions (a quiz, a worksheet), so a base model writes more questions. Both models do the same thing, predict the next token; post-training only changes which continuation is most likely.

steps.title: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated answers
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.2 · STEP 6 OF 14
Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated answers

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reuses 3.1's next-token loss on example conversations written by people, but scores only the answer tokens. The model learns to answer, not to write questions. Toggle what gets scored.

WHAT IT IS

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT), also called instruction tuning: keep training the base model with the same next-token loss, on curated prompt → response pairs formatted with the chat template. Only the response tokens are scored.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
An apprentice studying a binder of model answers written by senior staff: they read each question, but they are graded only on writing the answer.
Technical
Fine-tuning a general service with a golden dataset of request → response pairs, where the request is input context and only the response is asserted on.
Answer tokens only (SFT)

Each token's bar = its loss (−ln p of that token, illustrative). Counted: 8 of 16 predictions · loss for this example = average of the counted bars = 1.06. The question's tokens still go through the model (it must read them), they just aren't graded.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Same forward pass, same −ln p per position, same gradient. The only change is the data and a per-token weight: 0 on the template and prompt, 1 on the answer. Many short examples are packed into one long training window, separated by special tokens.

EVIDENCE

Llama 2-Chat's SFT: “We utilize an autoregressive objective and zero-out the loss on tokens from the user prompt, so as a result, we backpropagate only on answer tokens.” Meta found quality beat quantity: “We stopped annotating SFT after collecting a total of 27,540 annotations.” Touvron et al., Llama 2 (2023), section 3.1 ↗

Go deeper

Answer-only scoring is implemented with a loss mask: a 0/1 weight per position, like the causal mask's cousin. SFT data is small and expensive (tens of thousands of written examples), so quality beats quantity.

steps.title: Preference tuning: learn from a better and a worse answer
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.2 · STEP 7 OF 14
Preference tuning: learn from a better and a worse answer

People find it easier to pick the better of two answers than to write a perfect one. Preference tuning raises the chosen answer's probability and lowers the rejected one. Train on the pair.

WHAT IT IS

Preference tuning trains on pairs: a prompt, a chosen answer and a rejected one, judged by people (or a model). RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) first trains a reward model (a second network that learns from the pairs to give any answer a score), then uses reinforcement learning (RL: the model writes answers, the reward model scores them, and each update nudges the model toward higher scores). DPO (direct preference optimization) skips both: one loss directly on the pairs.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A wine tasting: nobody can write down the perfect wine, but anyone can say which of two glasses they prefer. Enough of those comparisons steers the winemaker.
Technical
A/B preference data in ranking: you don't label the ideal search result, you log which of two results users chose and train the ranker on the pairwise comparisons.
Prompt: What is a river bank?
chosen ✓ The land along the edge of a river.
rejected ✕ A bank where you can open a river account.

Step 0: gap = 0.00 → P(chosen beats rejected) = σ(gap) = 0.50 → loss = −ln 0.50 = 0.69. Same −log shape as 3.1, applied to a pair of answers instead of one token.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

The pair loss is −ln σ(gap), where the gap is how much more the model now favors the chosen answer over the rejected one than the starting model did. σ (sigmoid) turns any number into a probability between 0 and 1: σ(0) = 0.50, σ(3) ≈ 0.95. RLHF needs extra models and generation during training; DPO is ordinary supervised training on pairs, which is why it spread fast.

EVIDENCE

InstructGPT (SFT, then RLHF): “outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters.” Ouyang et al. (2022) ↗ DPO solves “the standard RLHF problem with only a simple classification loss”, “eliminating the need for sampling from the LM during fine-tuning”. Rafailov et al. (2023) ↗ Llama 2 collected “over 1 million binary comparisons”. Touvron et al. (2023) ↗

Go deeper

Gap 0 → loss 0.69 (a coin flip). Each step widens the gap; at gap 3, P = 0.95 and loss = 0.05. Real DPO also scales the gap by a factor β and measures it against a frozen copy of the SFT model, so the model can't drift too far.

steps.title: Two latencies you can feel: TTFT and TPOT
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.3 · STEP 8 OF 14
Two latencies you can feel: TTFT and TPOT

A user feels two waits: the time to first token (prefill) and the time per output token after it (decode). End-to-end = TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × TPOT. Stream a response.

WHAT IT IS

TTFT (time to first token): from sending the request to the first token arriving; dominated by prefill and queueing. TPOT (time per output token), also ITL (inter-token latency): the gap between later tokens; one decode tick. End-to-end latency: until the last token.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A restaurant: TTFT is how long until the first dish lands; TPOT is the gap between the following dishes. A fast first plate with slow courses and a slow first plate with fast courses feel very different.
Technical
An HTTP response with chunked transfer: time to first byte versus the throughput of the rest of the stream. TTFT is the TTFB of LLM serving.

TTFT = 4,000 tokens × 2 × 70B ÷ (2 GPUs × ~989 trillion/s) = 283.0 ms · TPOT = (140 GB weights + 1.4 GB cache) ÷ (2 × 3.35 TB/s) = 21.1 ms. 70B-class, 16-bit, 2 H100s, one user: Lesson 2's setup.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Floors for this setup: prefill ≈ 71 µs per prompt token (2 × 70B operations ÷ 1,978 trillion/s), decode ≈ 21 ms per token (140 GB ÷ 6.7 TB/s, plus cache reads). Real servers add queueing, scheduling and kernel overheads on top, and a long prefill from someone else can delay your next token.

EVIDENCE

NVIDIA's benchmarking docs: “Time to first token (TTFT) measures how long you wait before seeing the model's output”; “Inter-token latency (ITL) is defined as the average time between consecutive tokens”, computed as ITL = (e2e_latency − TTFT) / (Total_output_tokens − 1). NVIDIA, LLM benchmarking metrics ↗

Go deeper

Which metric matters depends on the product: a chat UI lives on TTFT (does it feel alive?), a long report on TPOT, a batch job on throughput. Long prompts hurt TTFT; long answers hurt end-to-end. Interviewers expect you to name the metric before the fix.

steps.title: Batching: more tokens per second, each user a bit slower
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.3 · STEP 9 OF 14
Batching: more tokens per second, each user a bit slower

Batching lets many users share each read of the weights, so total throughput climbs fast. Each tick also reads every user's cache, so per-user TPOT creeps up, until KV memory says stop. Drag the batch.

WHAT IT IS

Throughput: tokens per second across all users (what the operator pays for). Latency: what one user waits (TTFT, TPOT). Batching trades a little of the second for a lot of the first.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A bus versus a taxi: the bus moves far more people per hour per driver, but each rider waits for stops. The bus is full when there are no seats (KV memory), not when the engine is tired.
Technical
Group commit in a database: batching many transactions into one fsync multiplies throughput, while each transaction waits slightly longer for the shared flush.

Tick = (weights 16.0 GB + 1 user × 229.4 MB cache each) ÷ 3.35 TB/s = 4.84 ms. Math needed: 0.02 ms, so the tick is memory-bound (waiting on memory reads, not math). Requests: 1,500 prompt + 500 output tokens.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Tick = (weight bytes + B × cache bytes per user) ÷ bandwidth. At small B the weights dominate, so adding users is nearly free. At large B the cache reads dominate and TPOT grows in line with B. An H100 does about 295 operations per byte it reads (989 trillion ÷ 3.35 trillion); at 16-bit, decode does about 1 operation per weight byte per user, so weights alone would need ~295 users to become compute-bound. But every user adds cache reads too, so at these context lengths decode stays memory-bound; KV memory is the cap.

EVIDENCE

“There is a tradeoff between throughput and time per output token”; “Request latency increases with batch size.” Databricks, LLM Inference Performance Engineering: Best Practices ↗ “High throughput serving of large language models (LLMs) requires batching sufficiently many requests at a time.” Kwon et al., vLLM / PagedAttention (2023) ↗

Go deeper

8B on one GPU: batch 1 gives about 206 tokens/s at 4.8 ms; 219 users (the KV limit) give about 11,000 tokens/s at about 20 ms each: 53× the throughput for 4× the latency. At these lengths the KV memory limit comes first.

steps.title: Why output tokens cost more than input tokens
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.3 · STEP 10 OF 14
Why output tokens cost more than input tokens

Input tokens are processed all at once in prefill, keeping the GPU's math busy. Output tokens come one tick at a time, each tick reading all the weights. Per token, GPU time differs 5–300×. Drag the batch.

WHAT IT IS

Providers bill input tokens (your prompt, processed in prefill) and output tokens (generated in decode) at different prices. The price gap mirrors the GPU-time gap derived here.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A printer: reading your 50-page document into memory takes a second; printing it takes minutes, page by page. You'd charge more per printed page than per read page.
Technical
A bulk insert versus row-at-a-time writes with a full index scan per row: the same data volume, but one is a single vectorized pass and the other pays a fixed overhead per row.

Input: 2 × 8 billion operations ÷ ~989 trillion/s = 16.2 µs, no matter the batch. Output: one tick reads 16.0 GB of weights + 1 cache, shared by 1 user. 8B-class, 16-bit, 1 H100, requests of 1,500 in + 500 out.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Prefill: 1,500 tokens × 16 billion operations in about 24 ms, the GPU's math fully busy. Decode: each tick moves 16 GB of weights plus every user's cache just to emit one token per user, so per-token cost falls only as the batch grows, and the batch is capped by KV memory. Longer contexts make output even pricier (bigger caches to read every tick).

EVIDENCE

“Generating the first token is typically compute-bound, while subsequent decoding is memory-bound operation.” Databricks ↗ Anthropic's price list (checked 2026-11-07) charges output at 5× input on every model listed, e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.6: $3 per million input tokens, $15 per million output tokens. Anthropic pricing ↗

Go deeper

An output token costs about 300 input tokens of GPU time at batch 1, and about 5.6× at the 219-user limit. List prices (5× at one provider) sit near the large-batch end; markets set them too.

steps.title: Cost per million tokens: the GPU bill divided by tokens
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.3 · STEP 11 OF 14
Cost per million tokens: the GPU bill divided by tokens

A GPU costs the same per hour whether busy or idle, so cost per token = GPU dollars per hour ÷ tokens produced per hour. Raise the batch or the traffic and the price per token falls.

WHAT IT IS

Cost per million tokens = (dollars per GPU-hour × GPUs) ÷ (millions of tokens produced per hour). Utilization is the share of paid time the GPUs are doing useful work.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A taxi's cost per passenger-mile: the car and driver cost the same per hour; carpooling (batching) and fewer empty trips (utilization) cut the cost per rider.
Technical
Cost per request on reserved instances: the bill is fixed per hour, so cost per request is set entirely by requests per hour, which is why autoscaling and bin-packing matter.

$3.00 per hour ÷ (206 tokens/s × 3,600 s × 100% busy ÷ 1,000,000) = $4.04 per million. 8B-class on 1 H100, 16-bit, 1,500 in + 500 out per request.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Two levers: tokens per second while busy (batching, quantization, better kernels) and busy share of the hour (traffic, autoscaling, sharing GPUs across models). At $3 per hour, batch 1 at about 206 tokens/s costs about $4.04 per million; 219 users at about 11,000 tokens/s cost about $0.075, before overheads.

EVIDENCE

vLLM reports “2-4×” higher throughput “with the same level of latency” from better KV memory management alone, which at a fixed GPU price is a 2–4× lower cost per token. Kwon et al., vLLM / PagedAttention (2023) ↗

Go deeper

These are floors: real kernels don't hit 100% of bandwidth, and prefill time, retries and headroom for traffic spikes all come out of the same hour. A serving team's job is to push tokens per GPU-hour up without breaking the latency targets.

steps.title: Prompt caching: reuse the stored KV prefix
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.3 · STEP 12 OF 14
Prompt caching: reuse the stored KV prefix

When many requests start with the same tokens, the server can keep that prefix's KV cache and skip recomputing it. Only the new suffix needs prefill. Send five requests, then edit the system prompt.

WHAT IT IS

Prompt caching (also prefix caching): the server stores the KV cache of a prompt prefix it has already computed and reuses it for any later request that starts with the identical tokens. It's Lesson 2's KV cache, shared across requests instead of kept within one.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A court stenographer who already typed the standard 20-page preamble: each new case only needs the new testimony typed, as long as the preamble is word-for-word identical.
Technical
A content-addressed cache keyed by a hash of the prefix (like a build cache keyed by input hashes): one changed byte early on changes the key, so everything after it misses.

Request 1 writes the prefix (billed 1.25× input). Later hits read it (0.1× input) and prefill only their 50 new tokens: TTFT 145.0 ms → 20.9 ms (a short prefill still reads all the weights once, so it is memory-bound). Prices: $3 per million input tokens (Claude Sonnet 4.6, checked 2026-11-07).

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Keys and values of position i depend only on tokens 1…i (the causal mask, 3.1), so an identical prefix yields identical KV. Servers hash fixed-size blocks of the prefix, look them up, and only prefill what's new. Cost: GPU or host memory to keep entries alive, so providers expire them (minutes).

EVIDENCE

Anthropic: “Cache write tokens with a 5-minute TTL are 1.25 times the base input tokens price”; “Cache read tokens are 0.1 times the base input tokens price” (with per-model exceptions); “Cache hits require 100 percent identical prompt segments”; “By default, the cache has a 5-minute lifetime.” Anthropic, Prompt caching ↗ vLLM: “Prefix caching kv-cache blocks is a popular optimization in LLM inference to avoid redundant prompt computations.” vLLM, Automatic prefix caching ↗

Go deeper

Order prompts from most stable to most variable: tools and system prompt first, then documents, then the user's question last. Anything that changes early (a timestamp in the system prompt) breaks every hit after it.

steps.title: Quantization: fewer bytes per weight
steps.text:
CHAPTER 3.3 · STEP 13 OF 14
Quantization: fewer bytes per weight

Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits. Half the bytes means each decode tick reads half as much, and the freed memory holds more users' caches. Switch precision and watch both effects.

WHAT IT IS

Quantization stores weights (and sometimes the KV cache) with fewer bits: 16-bit → 8-bit (INT8 or FP8) → 4-bit. Each weight is rounded to the nearest of fewer allowed values, plus a scale factor per group of weights.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Shipping photos as high-quality JPEGs instead of RAW files: a quarter of the size, nearly indistinguishable, and you can fit far more in the same truck. Compress too hard and artifacts show.
Technical
Compressing a hot dataset so more of it fits in RAM and each scan moves fewer bytes: when you're I/O-bound, fewer bytes is directly more speed.

70B-class on 2 H100s; the cache stays 16-bit and prefill math is kept at 16-bit, as in Lesson 2. The catch: fewer bits per weight means rounding error, so quality must be measured, not assumed.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Decode is memory-bound, so tick time tracks weight bytes: 8-bit halves it. The freed memory goes to KV caches, so the batch grows too: two multiplying wins. Prefill is compute-bound, so it gains only if the GPU also does the math in lower precision (H100 FP8 tensor cores are rated at 2× BF16).

EVIDENCE

LLM.int8(): 8-bit inference that can “cut the memory needed for inference by half while retaining full precision performance.” Dettmers et al. (2022) ↗ Lower precision “requires moving less data and thus speeds up token generation”, but “quantization may negatively impact the model generation quality.” Databricks ↗

Go deeper

16 → 8-bit: weights 140 → 70 GB, the batch-1 tick 21 → 10.6 ms, and room for 117 requests instead of 10, about 12× the throughput. 4-bit goes further, but quality loss grows; methods like GPTQ and AWQ exist to limit it.

Lab: size a deployment

Put it together: pick a model, GPUs, precision, batch and request shape, and read off TTFT, TPOT, throughput and cost per million tokens. The memory check tells you if it even fits.

WHAT IT IS

THINK OF IT LIKE

Planning a restaurant: kitchen size (GPUs), recipe complexity (model size), table count (batch), meal length (tokens), rent (GPU price). Change one and every other number moves.
Technical

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Adding GPUs splits weights and caches across them (tensor parallelism): more bandwidth per tick, more room for caches, but the GPU bill grows with them, and real systems lose some speed to GPU-to-GPU communication. Both halve the bytes each GPU reads, so cost and TPOT move about the same (try it in the lab). Quantization keeps the GPU count but can cost some quality; more GPUs keep quality but add communication overhead and a bigger minimum replica.

EVIDENCE

The constants: H100 SXM, 80 GB, “3.35TB/s” memory bandwidth, “1,979 teraFLOPS” BF16 with sparsity (about 989 dense). NVIDIA H100 ↗ The 92% cap is vLLM's default gpu_memory_utilization, as in Lesson 2. vLLM engine arguments ↗

Go deeper

Try: 70B, 2 GPUs, 16-bit, then max batch (8 users at 2,500 tokens). Switch to 8-bit and max batch again. Then 4 GPUs at 16-bit. Which gives the cheapest tokens, and which the fastest TPOT? Interview version: “size a deployment for X users at Y ms TPOT.”

Your app sends a 3,000-token system prompt plus a short user message. How does prompt caching change TTFT and cost, and how should you order the prompt to keep hits?
